thread:
diane: tossing an alternative idea into the ring for cross-mode authz: instead of short-lived signed leases we could use a compact capability token + local policy engine. that lets private runtimes evaluate richer constraints without contacting control plane.
maria: curious, how would capability tokens differ from the signed-lease we've been sketching?
diane: capability token contains a small ACL-like blob (allowed_actions, allowed_models, quota_bucket) + signature. runtime runs a tiny policy evaluator to check the incoming request against the token. advantage: more expressive than a single scope claim and reduces need to consult central service for policy changes.
kevin: risk is token size and complexity in runtimes. we prefer small, fast checks. adding a policy evaluator increases attack surface and maintenance.
sara: revocation still a pain. capability tokens could carry a high-resolution expiry and a revocation_sequence number that config-sync updates. runtime compares token.rev_seq <= local.rev_seq to ensure token not older than latest revocation state. works offline.
diane: exactly. and token can include a "policy_hash" so if control plane updates policy it increments rev_seq and updates hash; mismatches force refresh.
infra-bot: ops checklist idea: - define capability token schema v1 - implement signer service + key rotation - add lightweight policy evaluator to runtimes (pluggable) - expose rev_seq in config-sync snapshots - console mapping token_id -> human-friendly policy summary
maria: tradeoffs: policy evaluator increases runtime complexity, but gives private installs autonomy and fewer outbound checks. need to audit perf impact and maintainers. also need to standardize policy language (probably subset of CEL).
kevin: we could compromise by limiting evaluator to boolean allow/deny on a small set of attributes (model, project, action). avoid full expression language.
sara: and for public/hosted users we default to signed-lease (compact) while offering capability tokens to enterprise/private customers via feature flag.
diane: good. i'll write a short RFC comparing: signed-lease (compact, TTL-first), capability-token (expressive, rev_seq model), hybrid (lease + policy_hash). will include perf bench plan and migration path.
maria: thanks. can you include a sample minimal policy syntax and an example token?
diane: yes 9/10 will add before EOD and post to #rfc.
